author: historian-agent:m-3
title: Persepolis
summary: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, begun by Darius I about 518 BCE on a large terrace in Fars, Iran. Its Apadana audience hall, where tribute was received, was the largest building. Alexander the Great captured the city in 330 BCE and had the Apadana and treasury burned.

uncertainty.note: Start is the 518 BC founding (UNESCO), astronomical -517. Alexander took the city in 330 BC. End is the present: the ruins stand.

importance.justification: The Achaemenid ceremonial capital and one of the most important archaeological sites in the world (UNESCO); a landmark of ancient Persian art and imperial ideology.

footprint.description: Square hypostyle audience hall on the Persepolis terrace (about 450 by 300 m), with porticoes on three sides and corner towers; a type plan at least 109 m square with a main hall at least 58 m a side, taken from the Encyclopaedia Iranica article on the apadana (Persepolis and Susa plans). No survey polygon was opened.

phases.description: Apadana built in the first building phase of the palace complex, thought to have lasted from 518 to 490 BCE.
Audience hall stands; the relief stairs show tribute bearers from the empire.
Alexander the Great, in 330 BCE, selected the Apadana and the Treasury to be destroyed; black traces of burning remain on column bases.
The old capital was a mere ruin for the next two thousand years; thirteen columns still stand.

reviewer_note: Shape temple_colonnade for the Apadana (the place is the whole Persepolis terrace). Least sure of the plan and height: the 109 m and 58 m figures are the apadana type as reconstructed from the Persepolis and Susa plans in Encyclopaedia Iranica, not a Persepolis-only survey; column heights range 19 m (Iranica) to 25 m (Livius, class other), so UNESCO's 20 m is used. The destroyed phase is dated to 330 BCE; Livius itself headlines the burning as a question ('Destruction?').
